The Sable antelope, Hippotragus niger, is a large-bodied ungulate inhabiting the miombo woodlands of sub-Saharan Africa, whose life-history traits reflect a slow pace of life typical of the Hippotragini tribe. Long-term field records from South African protected areas indicate that female calves are born after a gestation period of 271 days [tg = 271 days], a duration that remains consistent across populations when measured at a core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This relatively lengthy intrauterine development is characteristic of a species that invests heavily in a single precocial offspring, with the birth mass of female neonates recorded at approximately 16,375 grams [Wwb = approximately 16,375 grams], a substantial initial mass that underpins the calf’s rapid early mobility, an essential trait for evading predators in open savanna habitats. Such a high neonatal mass, sustained over a prolonged gestation, imposes considerable energetic demands on gravid females throughout the dry season, when forage quality often declines.

Sexual dimorphism in body size becomes markedly apparent as individuals approach adulthood, with the ultimate wet weight for males reaching 235,000 grams [Wwi = 235,000 grams], a figure significantly exceeding the 220,000 grams [Wwi = 220,000 grams] recorded for fully grown females. This pronounced size disparity, driven by intrasexual competition among males for access to receptive females, is a common pattern across the Bovidae. The data, collected from mature specimens in Kruger National Park, reflect the asymptotic mass attained once somatic growth is complete, typically after the sixth year of life. The sheer energetic cost of maintaining such a large frame, particularly for males, is thought to contribute to the species’ relatively extended developmental timelines, as resources must be diverted to structural growth before reproductive effort can be fully allocated.

The onset of reproductive capability follows distinct temporal trajectories for each sex, a pattern directly linked to the differing selective pressures experienced by males and females in a polygynous mating system. Under the species’ typical active body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], young females attain puberty at approximately 768 days since birth [tp = approximately 768 days since birth], enabling them to participate in breeding at around two years of age. In contrast, males experience a considerably prolonged period of sexual maturation, reaching puberty at roughly 1,184 days since birth [tp = roughly 1,184 days since birth] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This nearly 1.5-fold delay in male maturity is an adaptive response to the intense physical competition for dominance, as younger males rarely gain access to estrous females and instead benefit from continued somatic growth to enhance their future fighting ability.

The early-life developmental milestone of nutritional independence in this species is marked by weaning, which occurs at 213 days since birth [tx = 213 days since birth] at the standard core temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This age at weaning, typical of large-bodied grazing bovids, signals the point at which the calf transitions fully to a diet of roughage, relying on its developing rumen to digest fibrous grasses. Following this transition, the juvenile enters a prolonged period of growth and learning within the maternal herd, during which it refines its foraging skills and social knowledge before dispersing. The ability of a female to successfully rear a calf to this milestone is highly dependent on habitat quality, with calves born after dry years often exhibiting delayed weaning ages in some populations tracked by ongoing research.

Regarding the species’ ultimate longevity, the maximum lifespan recorded for Hippotragus niger has been documented at approximately 8,103 days [am = approximately 8,103 days], a figure derived from long-term individual monitoring in populations living at a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This total lifespan, equivalent to just over 22 years, is modest relative to some other large African ungulates but reflects the considerable mortality risks—including predation and drought-related starvation—that accumulate over a sable antelope’s lifetime. In terms of lifetime reproductive output, females achieve a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 1 calf per year [Ri = approximately 1 calf per year], producing a single calf per annual event [Ri = single calf per annual event]. This low rate, constrained by the high maternal investment in each calf, limits the species’ capacity for rapid population recovery following environmental perturbation.
